title: Heart and lungs on the clock: who sets the pace, and who holds it back?

summary.text: Your heart beats about 85 times a minute while you sit still. Yet a heart left on its own beats nearer 100. So something is holding yours back. You count your pulse before, during and after exercise, and measure your chest as you breathe. You find out how a nerve acts like a brake on the heart, why breathing is the one automatic job you can also take over, and how scientists first caught a nerve slowing an organ.
summary.art: A child sitting on a stair with two fingers on her wrist and a stopwatch beside her, while a faint drawing of her heart and lungs glows through her chest.

intro.hook: Put two fingers on your wrist and count the beats for 15 seconds. Now hold your breath for five seconds. Which of these two could you stop if you really wanted to?
intro.text: You can hold your breath, and you can breathe out slowly or sing a long note. You cannot decide to stop your heart. Yet both organs work all day and all night without you thinking about them. Why can you take over one and not the other? And what is your heart doing while you sit still and do nothing?
intro.art: A boy holding his nose and puffing out his cheeks, next to a drawing of a heart with a clock face on it.

outcomes: I can find my pulse, count it for 15 seconds, and work out beats per minute.
I can describe how my pulse rises when exercise starts and falls when it stops, and read this from a line graph.
I can explain that the heart has its own pacemaker, and that a nerve acts like a brake that keeps a resting heart slower than its own speed.
I can explain how breathing works: the diaphragm and rib muscles change the size of the chest, and the air outside flows in.
I can explain that breathing is automatic but can be taken over, and say what happens when I hold my breath.
I can sort body jobs into automatic only, automatic but steerable, and decided by me, and give a reason.
I can compare heart rates and breathing across people and other animals, and say what a bigger or smaller number tells us.
I can say how scientists found that a nerve can slow an organ, and which idea this proved wrong.

terms.meaning: The small push you can feel in an artery each time the heart beats. You can feel it on the inside of your wrist.
terms.example: Count the pushes under two fingers for 15 seconds, and you have counted your heartbeats.
terms.art: Two fingers resting on the inside of a wrist, with small ripples drawn under the skin.

terms.meaning: The number of heartbeats in one minute. It is the usual way to say how fast a heart is going.
terms.example: If you count 21 beats in 15 seconds, that is 21 times 4, which is 84 beats per minute.
terms.art: A stopwatch with a heart beside it and the number 84 on a card.

terms.meaning: Your pulse when you have been sitting or lying quietly for a few minutes. For most children aged 6 to 10 it is between about 70 and 110 beats per minute.
terms.example: Your resting pulse is lower when you wake up in bed than when you stand up fast.
terms.art: A child lying quietly on a mat with a calm heart drawn beside her.

terms.meaning: A small group of special cells at the top of the heart that start every heartbeat by themselves. Doctors call it the sinoatrial node.
terms.example: A heart taken out of a frog and kept in the right salty water goes on beating, because its pacemaker still works.
terms.art: A drawing of a heart with a small glowing patch at the top right and ripples spreading from it.

terms.meaning: A thin cable of living cells that carries signals between the brain and the rest of the body.
terms.example: A nerve carries the signal from your brain to your hand when you decide to pick up a cup.
terms.art: A white thread-like nerve running from a brain down through a neck and branching into a hand.

terms.meaning: A long nerve that runs from the brainstem down to the heart, lungs and gut. Its signals slow the heart. The name comes from a Latin word meaning wandering.
terms.example: When you sit quietly, the vagus nerve sends steady signals to your heart, and your pulse stays lower.
terms.art: A long wandering nerve drawn from the base of a brain down past the lungs to the heart and stomach.

terms.meaning: The part of the brain at the top of the neck, joining the brain to the spinal cord. It runs jobs you never think about, such as the rhythm of your breathing.
terms.example: Cells in your brainstem keep you breathing while you are fast asleep.
terms.art: A side view of a head with the brainstem coloured at the base of the brain.

terms.meaning: Something your body does by itself, without you deciding. Scientists also say involuntary.
terms.example: Your heartbeat, the squeeze of your gut and the widening of your eye's pupil in the dark are automatic.
terms.art: A body outline with small gears turning inside the chest and tummy.

terms.meaning: A very fast automatic reaction. It is often handled by the spinal cord before the brain has even heard about it.
terms.example: You pull your hand away from a hot tava before you feel the pain.
terms.art: A hand jerking back from a hot tava on a stove, with a small spark of signal along the arm.

terms.meaning: A big, dome-shaped sheet of muscle under your lungs. It is the main muscle for breathing in.
terms.example: When the diaphragm tightens and flattens, your lungs grow bigger and air flows in.
terms.art: A cut-away of a chest showing a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, flat on one side and domed on the other.

terms.meaning: The muscles between your ribs. They lift the ribs up and out as you breathe in.
terms.example: Put a hand on each side of your ribs and breathe in deeply. You feel them swing outwards.
terms.art: A rib cage drawn from the front, with arrows showing ribs swinging up and out like bucket handles.

terms.meaning: How many breaths you take in one minute. Breathing in and out once counts as one breath.
terms.example: A child at rest takes about 18 to 25 breaths per minute.
terms.art: A child with a hand on her tummy and a tally of tick marks beside her.

terms.meaning: How much air moves in and out with one breath. A deep breath moves much more air than a quiet one.
terms.example: After running, each breath is deeper as well as faster.
terms.art: Two balloons side by side, one small for a quiet breath and one big for a deep breath.

terms.meaning: The special muscle that makes up the heart. Unlike the muscles in your arm, it does not tire out in the same way, and it does not need a signal from the brain to beat.
terms.example: You can clench your fist until your arm aches, but your heart muscle goes on for a whole life.
terms.art: A close drawing of heart muscle fibres branching and joined end to end.

terms.meaning: A chemical that the body releases when you are excited, frightened or working hard. It makes the heart beat faster and harder.
terms.example: Your heart thumps at the top of a roller coaster because adrenaline has reached it.
terms.art: Two small glands on top of kidneys sending tiny dots along a blood vessel to a heart.

terms.meaning: The time your pulse and breathing take to come back down to normal after exercise.
terms.example: After fast step-ups, your pulse falls quickly in the first minute and then more slowly.
terms.art: A line graph of a pulse climbing steeply and then sliding down in a long curve.

explanations.concept: Pulse and heart rate: how to count the heart from your wrist
explanations.definition: The pulse is the push that each heartbeat sends along your arteries, and heart rate is how many beats there are in a minute.
explanations.description: Each time the heart squeezes, it pushes blood into the arteries, and the artery walls stretch for a moment. You feel that stretch as a small tap under two fingers on your wrist. To find the heart rate, count the taps for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Always use two fingers and not your thumb, because the thumb has a pulse of its own and can fool you. A miscount of one beat in 15 seconds becomes a mistake of 4 beats per minute, so scientists count the same way each time and repeat the count. Most children aged 6 to 10 have a resting pulse between about 70 and 110 beats per minute.
examples: 21 beats in 15 seconds is 84 beats per minute.
Counting the same way three times shows how much the number wobbles.
A grown-up's resting pulse is usually lower, about 60 to 90.
explanations.art: A wrist with two fingers on it, a stopwatch, and the sum 21 times 4 equals 84.

explanations.concept: The heart has its own pacemaker
explanations.definition: A small patch of special cells at the top of the heart, called the pacemaker or the sinoatrial node, starts each heartbeat by itself.
explanations.description: Your heart does not wait for a message from the brain to beat. Special cells in the pacemaker make a tiny electrical signal again and again. The signal spreads over the heart muscle, and the heart squeezes. A frog's heart taken out of the body and kept in the right salty water goes on beating for hours. A transplanted human heart has its nerves cut, and it still beats. Left alone, a human pacemaker fires at about 100 to 115 times a minute. That is faster than the resting pulse of most people, and this puzzle is what the next card answers.
examples: A frog's heart in salty water keeps beating on a laboratory dish.
After a heart transplant, the new heart beats with its nerves cut, usually at about 90 to 110 beats a minute at rest.
Heart cells grown in a dish beat by themselves, and cells that touch fall into the same rhythm.
explanations.art: A heart in a salty dish with ripples spreading out from a glowing patch at the top.

explanations.concept: The brake: why a resting heart is slower than its own speed
explanations.definition: The vagus nerve sends steady signals to the pacemaker that slow it down. This is why a resting heart beats more slowly than a heart on its own.
explanations.description: Imagine a bicycle with its brake lever held half on. The wheel could spin faster, but the brake holds it back. In a resting person, the vagus nerve is the brake on the heart. Its signals release a chemical onto the pacemaker cells, and the cells fire less often. When you start to move, the first thing that changes is that these signals ease off. This happens within a second or two, so the pulse jumps up very quickly. Then a second set of nerves and the chemical adrenaline press on the gas, and the pulse climbs higher. After exercise, the brake comes back fast, which is why the pulse falls steeply in the first minute.
examples: Your pulse rises in the first few seconds of a run, before your muscles have used up much oxygen.
After you stop, your pulse falls fastest in the first 30 to 60 seconds.
A transplanted heart has no vagus signals, so it beats at its own faster speed at rest.
explanations.art: A heart on a bicycle wheel, with a hand holding a brake lever on the left and a foot on a pedal on the right.

explanations.concept: Why the pulse rises fast at first and then slows down its climb
explanations.definition: Most of the rise in pulse at the start of exercise happens in the first 15 to 30 seconds, because easing the brake is quick. Later rises come from slower signals.
explanations.description: In the pulse timeline test, you meet a curve that rises steeply and then flattens. The steep part is the brake easing off, which takes a second or two. The slow part is adrenaline and the nerves that press the gas, plus the warming of your body. After you stop, the same happens in reverse. The brake returns quickly, so the pulse falls fast, and then the last part falls slowly because your body is still warm and still has adrenaline. In grown-ups, doctors sometimes time how far the pulse falls in the first minute as a rough sign of how fit the heart is. It is not a test for children.
examples: A child's pulse of 84 at rest may reach about 108 after only 15 seconds of step-ups.
After a minute of step-ups, it may be about 140 and climbing slowly.
In the first minute of rest, it may fall by 30 or more beats, and then fall only a little each minute.
explanations.art: A line graph that climbs steeply and then flattens, with the steep part labelled brake lets go and the flat part labelled gas pedal.

explanations.concept: The pulse is a wave, not the blood itself
explanations.definition: The pulse you feel in your wrist is a wave of stretch passing along the artery wall. It is not the same blood that left the heart a moment ago.
explanations.description: When the heart squeezes, it pushes a bit of blood into the aorta, the biggest artery. The elastic wall stretches and then springs back, and that stretch runs along all the arteries like a ripple along a rope you flick. The ripple moves at about 5 to 10 metres per second. That is much faster than the blood itself, which moves at well under one metre a second in the aorta and much more slowly in small vessels. So your wrist feels the tap almost at once, though the blood from that beat takes much longer to arrive.
examples: A flick along a long rope sends a ripple down it, though the rope itself does not travel.
A Mexican wave in a stadium runs round the stand, though no person runs round.
A doctor can feel a pulse at the ankle almost as soon as at the neck.
explanations.art: A rope being flicked at one end with a ripple travelling along it, and below it an artery with a stretch wave moving along the wall.

explanations.concept: How you breathe: muscles change the size of your chest
explanations.definition: You breathe in when the diaphragm and the rib muscles make your chest bigger. The air pressure outside then pushes air into your lungs.
explanations.description: The diaphragm tightens and flattens downwards, and the rib muscles lift your ribs up and out like the handles of a bucket. The space in the chest grows, so the pressure inside drops a little below the pressure of the air outside. The air outside then flows in. The lungs have no muscle of their own, and they are pushed out by the larger chest. When you breathe out quietly, the muscles relax and the stretched lungs and chest spring back, like a squeezed sponge. After hard exercise, your belly muscles help push the air out faster. At rest, a child aged 6 to 10 takes about 18 to 25 breaths a minute.
examples: Put a tape measure round your chest, and it grows when you breathe in.
A baby breathes mostly with the belly, as the diaphragm pulls down.
A frog breathes in a different way and gulps air down with its throat.
explanations.art: Two side views of a chest, one breathing in with a flat diaphragm and lifted ribs, and one breathing out with a domed diaphragm.

explanations.concept: Rate and depth: two ways to breathe more
explanations.definition: You can take more air in a minute by breathing faster, by breathing deeper, or both.
explanations.description: Breathing rate is how many breaths there are in a minute. Breath depth is how much air each breath moves. In gentle exercise, you mostly breathe deeper. In hard exercise, you breathe both deeper and faster. A fit person can move about ten times more air a minute in a sprint than while sitting still. Because the depth changes so much, counting breaths alone does not tell you how much air is moving. This is one reason the chest tape test is useful, because the tape shows the depth.
examples: Sitting: about 20 breaths a minute, each one quiet.
Walking fast: a similar number of breaths, but each is deeper.
Running hard: more than 40 breaths a minute, each one deep.
explanations.art: Three children from sitting to running, each with a balloon in front of her getting bigger and a tally of breaths getting longer.

explanations.concept: Automatic, but you can take over: who runs your breathing?
explanations.definition: Groups of nerve cells in the brainstem keep your breathing rhythm going without you. The thinking part of the brain can also take over the breathing muscles for a while.
explanations.description: In 1991, a team led by Jack Feldman found a small group of cells in the brainstem of mammals that set the rhythm of breathing. These cells keep going while you sleep. Sensors in your neck and brain measure the carbon dioxide in your blood, and if it rises, the rhythm speeds up. When you speak, sing, sigh or hold your breath, the thinking part of your brain sends its own signals to the same muscles. You can hold your breath for a short while, but as carbon dioxide builds up, the urge to breathe becomes strong. In normal air, the urge nearly always wins first, so you breathe before you faint. Never breathe fast and deep before holding your breath, because that can make you faint, especially in water.
examples: Breathing goes on in your sleep, and you cannot forget to do it.
You choose to breathe out in a long note when you sing.
A swimmer holds her breath for a few seconds, and then the urge to breathe forces her to come up.
explanations.art: A brainstem with a small drum-like rhythm maker, with one signal path to the breathing muscles from the base and another from the top of the brain.

explanations.concept: The pulse dances with your breath. Nobody agrees on why.
explanations.description: Look closely at a young person's pulse. It speeds up a little as they breathe in and slows down a little as they breathe out. Doctors call this respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and it is strongest in children and young adults and in slow, relaxed breathing. It is a normal and healthy sign. The fact is settled. The reason is not. Scientists have three main ideas, and each may be partly right.
examples: Slow breathing at about 6 breaths a minute makes the dance biggest.
The dance is usually smaller in older people.
It is hard to feel by hand, and a heart monitor shows it clearly.
explanations.art: A line of heartbeats drawn closer together on the in-breath and further apart on the out-breath, above a rising and falling breath line.

perspectives.who: Match the blood to the air
perspectives.explanation: More beats while the lungs are full of fresh air might pick up more oxygen in each minute, and fewer beats when the lungs are emptying might save energy. A 1996 study by Hayano and others, in dogs, found that the lungs swapped gases a little better when the heart rate followed the breath.

perspectives.who: A leak between two brain circuits
perspectives.explanation: The brainstem circuits that run breathing sit right next to those that send the brake signal to the heart. Perhaps the breathing circuit simply leaks into the brake as it works, with no purpose.

perspectives.who: A sign of a flexible body
perspectives.explanation: A heart that can speed up and slow down quickly is a heart with good control. Perhaps the dance does not do a job, but it shows that the brake and the gas are working well.

explanations.concept: The dive reflex: a brake you can borrow
explanations.definition: When cold water touches the face, and especially when the breath is held, the heart slows down. This is called the dive reflex.
explanations.description: Seals, dolphins and whales slow their hearts a lot on a deep dive, which saves oxygen. Humans have a smaller version. Cold water on the face sets off a reflex that increases the brake on the heart, and the pulse can fall by about a tenth or more in many people. This is the same vagus nerve doing its work. It is a reason why washing your face in cool water can feel calming. Never test it by putting your face in water without a grown-up beside you.
examples: A blue whale's heart has been recorded as slow as about 2 beats a minute during a deep feeding dive.
A cool damp cloth on the face can slow the pulse a little in many people.
A swimmer's pulse often drops a little when her face goes into cool water.
explanations.art: A blue whale diving with a slow heartbeat line beside it, next to a child holding a cool cloth to her face.

explanations.definition: The smaller an animal is, the faster the heart usually beats. Heart rates run from a few beats a minute to over a thousand.
explanations.description: An elephant's heart beats about 30 times a minute at rest. A person's beats about 70. A cat's beats about 150. A mouse's heart beats about 500 to 700 times a minute, and a hummingbird's can pass 1,000 in flight. Small bodies lose heat quickly and burn food fast, so their cells need oxygen very quickly. A blue whale is the other extreme. Scientists tagged blue whales in 2019 and recorded heart rates as slow as about 2 beats a minute during deep dives, and up to about 37 at the surface. Not every animal has a heart like ours. An insect has a long tube-shaped heart and breathes through tiny tubes that carry air to every part, so the blood does not need to carry oxygen. An octopus has three hearts.
examples: An elephant: about 30 beats a minute.
A cat: about 150 beats a minute.
A mouse: about 600 beats a minute.
A hummingbird in flight: more than 1,000 beats a minute.
explanations.art: A row of animals from elephant to mouse to hummingbird with a heart and a number above each.

agreed.text: The heart starts its own beat. Its pacemaker cells fire without any signal from the brain.
agreed.evidence: Hearts taken out of animals and kept in salty water go on beating. Transplanted human hearts, whose nerves are cut, go on beating in their new owners.

agreed.text: The vagus nerve acts as a brake on the heart, and it is on in a resting person.
agreed.evidence: A transplanted heart with no vagus nerve beats faster at rest than a normal heart. Also, a drug that blocks the vagus signal speeds up the resting pulse.

agreed.text: Nerves can slow an organ as well as speed it up, and they do so by releasing chemicals.
agreed.evidence: In 1921, Otto Loewi showed that fluid from a slowed frog heart could slow a second frog heart. The chemical was later named acetylcholine.

agreed.text: Breathing is made by the diaphragm and rib muscles, and the rhythm is set by cells in the brainstem.
agreed.evidence: Chest measurements show the ribs swinging out. Cutting the connection between the brainstem and the breathing muscles stops breathing, and a team led by Jack Feldman located the rhythm cells in 1991.

agreed.text: The urge to breathe comes mostly from rising carbon dioxide, not from falling oxygen.
agreed.evidence: Experiments with changed air mixtures show that extra carbon dioxide gives a strong urge to breathe, while a small fall in oxygen gives very little.

agreed.text: Pulse and breathing both rise within seconds when exercise starts, and both fall back over several minutes.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of children and adults in exercise tests show the same pattern in every healthy person.

challenging.claim: Your heart speeds up only after your muscles run low on oxygen.
challenging.who: Many people, and some old textbooks.
challenging.for: Oxygen and carbon dioxide levels do matter, and they take over the steady control of pulse a little later in exercise.
challenging.against: The pulse rises within the first few seconds, long before muscles run low. In some people it even rises before they move, while they wait for a race to begin. The first jump is the brake easing off.

challenging.for: The heart beats from before birth to the end of life without a long break.
challenging.against: Between every beat, the heart muscle relaxes. At rest, a little more than half of each beat's time is spent relaxed. This pause is also when the heart's own blood vessels fill with blood to feed it.

challenging.claim: Some yogis can stop their hearts at will.
challenging.who: Popular stories, and some early reports.
challenging.for: Some practised people can lower their pulse and breathing a great deal.
challenging.against: In 1961, Wenger, Bagchi and Anand tested yogis in India with heart-recording machines. They found that people could slow their pulse and make it hard to feel by tightening chest muscles and holding their breath, but the machine still showed the heart's own signals.

challenging.claim: You cannot change your heartbeat by thinking, because it is automatic.
challenging.for: You cannot stop your heart, or make it beat a set number of times, by simply deciding.
challenging.against: Slow breathing, a scary thought, a calm one, and the start of a race all change the pulse. You steer it by other routes, not by command.

challenging.claim: A lower resting pulse always means a healthier person.
challenging.for: Athletes often have low resting pulses, because a trained heart pushes out more blood with each beat.
challenging.against: Children normally have higher resting pulses than grown-ups. A very low pulse can also come from illness or some medicines. The number is only a clue, and a doctor looks at more than one.

big_questions.q: Your heart left alone would beat at about 100, yet yours beats at about 85, so something is holding it back all your life. Who or what decides how hard to hold the brake?
big_questions.hint: Think about which parts of the body measure things, and which parts send signals.

big_questions.q: When you hold your breath, who is doing the holding, and who is the one that gasps at the end? Are they both you?
big_questions.hint: Think about which one of you decided, and which one did not.

big_questions.q: Imagine that you had to remember to make every heartbeat yourself. What would sleeping be like? What would an automatic heart let you do instead?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your attention is free to do because the heart looks after itself.

big_questions.q: A hummingbird's heart beats over 1,000 times a minute and a blue whale's sometimes 2 times. Do they live at different speeds of time?
big_questions.hint: Some scientists have noticed that many mammals have a similar number of heartbeats in a lifetime. This idea is debated, and some animals break the pattern.

big_questions.q: The pulse in your wrist is a wave, not the blood itself. What else do we feel as a thing, when it is really a wave passing through something else?
big_questions.hint: Think of a sound, a Mexican wave in a stadium or a ripple on a pond.

big_questions.q: A frog's heart on a laboratory dish goes on beating. Is that heart alive, or is only the frog alive? Where does one living thing stop and the next begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the heart cells in a dish that fall into the same rhythm as they touch.

big_questions.q: Fear speeds up your pulse before you have decided to be afraid. Do feelings begin in the body and reach the mind, or begin in the mind and reach the body?
big_questions.hint: William James thought the body came first, and Walter Cannon thought both came together. Scientists still argue.

big_questions.q: Every creature has its own clock for its heart and its breath. If a mouse and a whale could compare their worlds, what would each one find strange?
big_questions.hint: Think about what it is like to live where one heartbeat lasts a tenth of a second, or a half a minute.

story.title: Before the First Stroke
story.note: A made-up story. The girls, the boat and the regatta are imagined, though snake-boat and small-boat races on the lakes near Alappuzha at Onam are real. The science is real: a pulse can rise in someone who is waiting for a race to start, and a pulse falls quickly in the first minute after hard exercise.
text: Anju was nine, and she was the only person in the boat shed who was not rowing. She sat on an upturned bucket with a stopwatch in one hand and a notebook on her knee. Sheela Miss had set the class a task for Onam week. Count the pulse of five people, and write down what you notice.

Outside, the lake lay flat and bright. In two hours, her cousin Revathi's team would race in the Onam regatta at Punnamada. Twelve girls would row a long, slim boat painted banana yellow, and Manu would beat the drum to give them the rhythm. Revathi sat at the back and steered. She was eighteen, with a loud laugh and arms like coconut-tree trunks.

Last year the yellow boat had led for the first minute. Then it had faded, and it had finished fourth. Nobody on the team knew why. Revathi said it was the water. Manu said it was the wind. Ammamma said it was because they had skipped breakfast.
'Count mine first,' said Revathi, holding out her wrist. 'It will be boring. I am never nervous.'
Anju laid two fingers where Sheela Miss had shown her. She felt the small tap, tap, tap. She watched the stopwatch and counted. 'Twenty,' she said. 'Times four. Eighty.'
'You see? Boring,' said Revathi, and she went back to oiling her oar.
Anju wrote it down. 80, in the shed, sitting.

An hour later, the boats were drifting into line on the lake. Anju had been allowed into the little support boat, and Uncle Babu steered it close to the yellow stern, where Revathi sat very straight, staring at the water ahead. The starter stood on a launch with a flag. Nobody spoke.
'Revathi chechi,' whispered Anju. 'Please. For school. Give me your wrist.'

Revathi sighed and held it out without looking. Anju found the tap. It was quick and hard, like a bird knocking on a window. She counted for fifteen seconds. 'Thirty-three,' she said. 'Times four.' She stopped. 'One hundred and thirty-two.'
'Nonsense,' said Revathi. 'You counted it wrong. I am sitting still. Nothing has happened yet.'
'Nothing has happened,' said Anju, 'and it is one hundred and thirty-two.'

Then the flag dropped. The drum began and the oars bit the water. The yellow boat leapt forward and led for a while, and then, a minute later, it began to fade. Anju watched from the support boat with a lump in her throat. The yellow boat finished fourth, again.

When it was over, the rowers lay across their oars, gasping. Anju climbed onto the yellow boat and did what she had promised Sheela Miss. She counted Revathi's pulse in four short spells, one straight after the other, each for fifteen seconds. Forty-four. Thirty-eight. Thirty-four. Thirty-one. She wrote down the numbers and did the sums, and her pencil stopped on the page.

That afternoon, in the boat shed, she showed the notebook to Revathi. 'Eighty in the shed. One hundred and thirty-two at the start line, before anyone had moved. Then one hundred and seventy-six, one hundred and fifty-two, one hundred and thirty-six, one hundred and twenty-four.'
Revathi read the page twice. 'Before we moved?' she said. 'My heart was racing before the flag?'
'Sheela Miss says the body gets ready before you do anything,' said Anju. 'I think it was not boring. I think it was the opposite.'

Revathi was quiet for a long time. Then she looked up, and Anju saw her face change. 'Anju. At the start, we pull to the beat in our chests, don't we? Not to Manu's drum. The beat in my chest was one hundred and thirty-two. Manu's drum is slower. We go off too fast, like a pot boiling over, and by the time we are halfway there is nothing left.'
'So?' said Anju.

'So tomorrow,' said Revathi, 'for the first twenty strokes, Manu will beat the drum slower than feels right. And every rower will breathe out slowly on each stroke. We will row to the drum and not to our hearts.'

The final was the next morning. Anju stood on the wooden jetty at the finish, with her notebook pressed to her chest. When the flag dropped, the yellow boat started so slowly that people on the bank laughed. The other boats shot past it. But the yellow boat kept the same steady beat, stroke after stroke. At the halfway buoy, the other boats began to slow. The yellow boat did not. It crept past one boat, then another, then another.
It came second, by half a boat length, and it was the best finish in five years. Revathi lay back in the stern with her hand over her heart, laughing so hard she could not speak.

That night, Anju opened her notebook to a clean page. She wrote the title in big letters: THE BODY STARTS THE RACE BEFORE YOU DO. Then she wrote underneath, in small letters: But you can still choose the beat.
story.epiphany: Revathi's heart had started the race before she had moved a single muscle.
ask: Why might a body get ready for something before the thing has started? What could be the use of that?
How could you test whether your own pulse rises before you do something important, such as a race or a test?
If you row to the beat in your chest, what can go wrong? How could a drum or a slow breath help?

A slim yellow boat with twelve rowers waiting on a still lake at dawn, with a starter on a launch holding a flag.
A small support boat beside the yellow boat's stern, and a girl holding a rower's wrist while counting.

games.title: Who Is in Charge? A card game about body jobs
games.context: This is a sorting game about control. Each card names a job your body does. You decide whether the job is automatic only, automatic but you can take over, or decided by you.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with three tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.
