printables.title: 12 tokens: four of each of three kinds
items: Automatic, but I can take over
Automatic, but I can take over
Automatic, but I can take over
Automatic, but I can take over

rules: Each card names one job of a body. Decide who is in charge of that job.
There are three kinds. Automatic only means you cannot decide it. Automatic, but I can take over means it runs by itself, and you can also do it on purpose. I decide means you choose it.
Each player has three tokens, one of each kind. On your own, say your answer out loud instead.
The reader reads only the front of a card. Everyone puts one token face down, then turns it over together.
The reader reads the back. Each player with the right kind scores one point. If nobody is right, talk about why.
The next reader sits to the left. When all the cards are read, the player with the most points wins. On your own, count how many you got right, and try to beat that number another day.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile, face down. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: We will sort the jobs of a body. For each job, we decide who is in charge. Take one token of each kind.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take one token of each kind.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Who Is in Charge game. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: Cutting 36 pieces takes a while: a grown-up cuts, or the child uses blunt-ended scissors with an adult beside them. No printer? Copy each card on a scrap of paper, and use any three small things, such as a coin, a pebble and a bottle cap, as the three tokens. Up to 4 players share one set; the reader rotates.

flow.do: Read the three kinds of token aloud. Then read one practice card together, and ask the child to explain the choice before turning it over.
flow.say: Automatic only means you cannot decide it. Automatic but steerable means it runs itself, and you can take over. Let us try one card together.
flow.kid: Read the three kinds. Try one card together. Say why you chose your token.

ask.q: Which kind do you think breathing is, and why?
good: Automatic but I can take over, because I can hold my breath.
Both, because it works by itself and I can also change it.

flow.parent: Do not explain the card first. Any choice with a reason is a good start. Breathing is the central example of the game.
flow.context: In this step you practise with one card, and learn what the three kinds of token mean.

flow.do: Play the cards one at a time. The reader reads the front, everyone puts a token down, and the reader reads the back. Keep score.
flow.say: Read the front only. Put your token down face down. Turn them over together. Then I will read the back.
flow.kid: Read a front. Put a token down. Turn them over. Read the back.

ask.q: Which card surprised you most, and why?
good: The hiccups card, because it is the diaphragm.
Blinking, because I can do both.
The heartbeat, because I cannot decide it.

flow.parent: When a card is argued over, ask the player for the reason before reading the back. A good reason matters more than the point.
flow.context: In this step you play through the cards. You decide who is in charge of each job and check the back.

flow.do: Count the points. Put the cards marked Automatic, but you can take over in a row, and read their fronts aloud.
flow.say: Look at the jobs in the middle kind. Which of these is also in the other body jobs we met today?
flow.kid: Find the cards in the middle kind. What do they have in common?

ask.q: What do the middle cards have in common?
good: They all work by themselves but I can change them.
They all use muscles I can also move on purpose.
They are jobs that matter for staying alive and also for speaking or feeling.

flow.context: In this step you look at the cards in the middle kind, the jobs that run by themselves but can be steered.

flow.do: Ask the question below, and let the child think before giving any answer. Write down what the child says.
flow.say: Your heart is automatic only, and your breathing is automatic but steerable. Why do you think the body is built this way?
flow.kid: The heart is automatic only. Breathing is steerable. Why might that be?

ask.q: Why might breathing be steerable when the heart is not?
good: We need to speak and sing.
We need to hold our breath in water.
We need to cough to clear our throat.

flow.think: If the heart worked only when you decided, what would happen when you fell asleep?
flow.parent: Possible answers: breathing is needed for speech, swallowing, coughing and diving, and the heart has no such jobs. Many other answers are fine.
flow.context: In this last step you think about why the body is built this way.

experiments.title: Pulse Timeline: how fast does your pulse rise and fall?
experiments.question: How quickly does your pulse rise in the first seconds of exercise, and how quickly does it fall after you stop?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After only 15 seconds of step-ups, will your pulse be a little higher or a lot higher than at rest? After you stop, will it fall quickly at first or slowly at first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same child does every round, on the same step, at one step-up every two seconds. The child rests for at least 2 minutes before each round, until the pulse is back within 4 beats a minute of the rest number. The same person counts every time, on the same wrist, with two fingers, for exactly 15 seconds. Only one thing changes between rounds, which is how long the child exercises: 15, 30 or 60 seconds.

materials.item: a phone or kitchen clock with a stopwatch
a low, sturdy step about 20 centimetres high, such as the bottom stair
a chair for resting
a notebook and a pencil, with the results table drawn in the notebook
graph paper or squared paper

experiments.safety: Use a low, firm step with nothing slippery on it, and keep a grown-up beside the child. Stop at once if the child feels dizzy, has pain in the chest or cannot catch their breath. A child with a heart or breathing condition should ask the doctor first.
experiments.record: Write the beats in 15 seconds at rest, after 15, 30 and 60 seconds of step-ups, in the four windows after the last round, and at 2 and 3 minutes of rest. Multiply by 4 for each. Draw one line graph for the rise and a second for the fall.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you count your pulse at rest, after 15, 30 and 60 seconds of step-ups, and every 15 seconds after you stop. You find out when your pulse changes most.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with two fingers on her wrist, while a parent holds a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Sit quietly for 2 minutes. Then count your pulse for 15 seconds.

setup.art: The same child stepping up and down on the bottom stair, with a parent counting the seconds out loud.
setup.caption: 2. Step up and down for 15 seconds. Stop and count your pulse for 15 seconds.

setup.art: The child sitting on the chair for 2 minutes, with a parent writing numbers in a notebook table.
setup.caption: 3. Rest on the chair until your pulse is back near the rest number.

setup.art: The child stepping again for 30 seconds, and then for 60 seconds, with a stopwatch showing the time.
setup.caption: 4. Repeat with 30 seconds of step-ups, and then with 60 seconds.

setup.art: After the last round, the child counting four short windows in a row, with the parent writing the four numbers.
setup.caption: 5. After the 60 seconds, count four windows of 15 seconds, one straight after the other.

flow.do: Show the child the results table. Ask for a guess and a reason for the rise and for the fall. Write both down before any counting.
flow.say: We will count your pulse at rest, after a short burst of step-ups, and every 15 seconds after you stop. What do you think will happen, and why?
flow.kid: We will count your pulse many times. What do you think will happen? Why?

ask.q: After only 15 seconds of step-ups, will your pulse be a little higher or a lot higher? Why?
good: A lot higher, because the heart starts at once.
A little higher, because my muscles have not used much yet.
It depends on how fast I step.

ask.q: After you stop, will it fall fast at first or slowly at first? Why?
good: Fast, because the heart wants to settle.
Slowly, because my body is still warm.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guess at the top of the page. One child: the parent times and writes. Two to four children: take turns as stepper, counter-and-timer, and recorder. Each child does their own full set of rounds with their own table and graph, and the others use the rest time to rest, count their own resting pulse or draw. Do not let two children step at once on one stair. The whole test takes about an hour, so it can be split into two sittings, with 15 and 30 seconds first and 60 seconds later.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pulse Timeline test. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Show the child how to rest two fingers on the thumb side of the wrist. Practise two counts of 15 seconds while the child sits still.
flow.say: Rest two fingers on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb. Press gently until you feel a tap. Do not use your thumb.
flow.kid: Put two fingers on your wrist, below the thumb. Press gently. Feel a tap.

check.q: Two practice counts are 20 and 21 beats in 15 seconds. What does this tell you?
options: You counted well, because the two numbers are close
You counted wrongly, because the numbers are not the same
check.why: A heart at rest has a steady pulse, and a difference of one beat is normal. If the two counts had differed by 5 or more, the finger spot or the counting method would need to change. If you picked the second option, remember that tiny differences are normal.

flow.parent: If the child cannot find the pulse, try the side of the neck, just under the jaw. Use two fingers there and press very gently.
flow.context: In this step you find your pulse and practise counting for 15 seconds.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit quietly for 2 minutes. Count the pulse for 15 seconds, wait a minute, and count again. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Sit still and breathe normally for two minutes. I will say start and stop. Count your taps for 15 seconds.
flow.kid: Sit still for 2 minutes. Count your pulse for 15 seconds. Write it down.
flow.parent: These two counts give the rest number. If they differ by more than 2, take a third and use the middle one.
flow.context: In this step you find your pulse at rest, which is the number to compare everything with.

flow.do: Ask the child to step up and down at one step-up every two seconds for exactly 15 seconds. Stop at once and count the pulse for 15 seconds. Write the number.
flow.say: Step up and down for fifteen seconds. When I say stop, count your taps right away for fifteen seconds.
flow.kid: Step up and down for 15 seconds. Stop. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.

ask.q: What did you notice in your chest?
good: It is not much faster yet.

flow.parent: Count right away, because the pulse starts to fall within seconds. This count is a little lower than the true peak. After the count, the child sits for 2 to 3 minutes. Take a 15-second count near the end to check that it is back near the rest number.
flow.context: In this step you do 15 seconds of step-ups and count your pulse straight away.

flow.do: When the pulse is back near the rest number, ask the child to step up and down for 30 seconds. Count the pulse for 15 seconds straight away. Write it down.
flow.say: Same step, same pace, but thirty seconds this time. Count your taps as soon as I say stop.
flow.kid: Step for 30 seconds. Stop. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.parent: If the child is tired or the pulse has not settled after 3 minutes, wait a little longer. A rest of 3 to 4 minutes is fine.
flow.context: In this step you do 30 seconds of step-ups, to see how the pulse grows as you keep going.

flow.do: When the pulse is back near the rest number, ask the child to step for 60 seconds. At once count the pulse for four windows of 15 seconds in a row. Write four numbers.
flow.say: Step for one full minute. When I say stop, count for fifteen seconds. Then I say new window, and you count again from zero.
flow.kid: Step for 1 minute. Stop. Count 15 seconds. Say the number. Count again.

ask.q: Which window had the most beats, and which had the fewest?
good: The first has the most, the last has the fewest.

flow.parent: The child says each number out loud at the end of its window, and a grown-up writes it down. Do not pause between windows. A fast pulse is hard to count, so count together for the first window. All pulse numbers in this experiment are typical, not promises. Children differ, so your own rise may be smaller or bigger.
flow.context: In this step you do one full minute of step-ups. Then you count four short windows, one after another, to see how the pulse falls.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit quietly. At 2 minutes and at 3 minutes after stopping, count the pulse for 15 seconds. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Sit and rest. At two minutes and at three minutes, we count again for fifteen seconds.
flow.kid: Rest on the chair. Count your pulse at 2 minutes and at 3 minutes.
flow.context: In this step you count at 2 and 3 minutes after you stop, to see the slow end of the fall.

flow.do: Help the child multiply every count by 4. Draw a line graph of the rise, with seconds of exercise along the bottom: 0, 15, 30, 60. Draw a second graph of the fall.
flow.say: Multiply each count by four to get beats per minute. Now plot the rise and the fall as two lines.
flow.kid: Multiply each count by 4. Draw two line graphs, one for rising and one for falling.

check.q: A child counted 28 beats in 15 seconds. What is that in beats per minute?
check.why: There are four 15-second spells in one minute. 28 times 4 is 112. If you chose 43, you added 15 instead of multiplying.

flow.context: In this step you turn your counts into beats per minute and draw two line graphs.

flow.do: Ask the child to write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Compare the claim with the first guess. Do not explain until the child has said what they think.
flow.say: What do you think happened to your pulse? What numbers show it? Why do you think your heart did that?
flow.kid: Write what you think, what you saw and why. Compare it with your guess.

ask.q: In which stretch did your pulse change the most?
good: In the first 15 seconds of stepping.
In the first 15 seconds after stopping.

ask.q: Why do you think it changed so fast at the start?
good: Something tells it to speed up before muscles run out of oxygen.

flow.parent: Expect the pulse to rise by roughly 20 to 30 beats a minute in the first 15 seconds, and then to climb more slowly. After stopping, expect the biggest fall in the first 30 to 60 seconds. Counts wobble by a few beats, so look at the shape and not at single numbers. Do not explain the brake until the child has made a claim.
flow.context: In this step you decide what your numbers show and why, before anyone explains.

experiments.title: The Chest Tape: how far does your chest move when you breathe?
experiments.question: How much does your chest grow when you breathe in, in a quiet breath, a deepest breath, and a deepest breath while slumped?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which breath will make your chest grow the most? Will sitting slumped make a difference? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same grown-up reads the tape every time. The tape goes round the chest just under the armpits, over a thin vest, at the same height each time. The child sits on the same chair, and only the way of breathing changes: quiet, deepest breath sitting straight, or deepest breath slumped.

materials.item: a soft tailor's tape measure, or a piece of string and a ruler
a chair without arms
a notebook and a pencil, with the results table drawn in the notebook

experiments.safety: Hold the tape snug and never tight. Stop if the child feels dizzy, and rest with normal breathing. Do not do more than three deep breaths in a row.
experiments.record: Write the chest size after breathing out and after breathing in, twice for each kind of breath. Work out the growth. Write which breath grew the most.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you measure your chest with a tape while you breathe. You find out how far the ribs swing out, and whether sitting slumped makes a difference.

setup.art: A child sitting straight on a chair while a parent holds a tailor's tape round her chest just under her armpits.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the tape round the chest, just under the armpits.

setup.art: The parent reading the tape at the front after the child has breathed out quietly.
setup.caption: 2. Read the tape at the end of a quiet breath out.

setup.art: The same child taking her deepest breath in, with the tape stretched wider and the parent reading it.
setup.caption: 3. Read the tape at the top of a breath in.

setup.art: The child slumped forward on the chair, taking a deepest breath, with the parent reading the tape.
setup.caption: 4. Repeat the deepest breath while slumped.

flow.do: Show the child the results table. Ask for a guess and a reason about which breath will grow the chest most, and about slumping. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will measure your chest with a tape while you breathe. Which breath will grow your chest the most? Does slumping matter? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will measure your chest while you breathe. Which breath grows it most? Why?

ask.q: Will slumping make your deepest breath bigger, smaller or the same? Why?
good: Smaller, because my ribs get squashed.
The same, because the lungs are the same size.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. One child: the parent holds the tape and writes. Two to four children: one is measured, one reads the tape, one writes, and then swap. Every child gets their own row of the table, and each reader should use the same reading spot on the tape every time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Chest Tape test. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Put the tape round the chest just under the armpits, over a thin vest. Hold it snug and not tight. Practise reading it at the end of a normal breath out.
flow.say: The tape goes just under your armpits. I will hold it snug, not tight. Breathe normally while I practise reading it.
flow.kid: Stand still. A grown-up holds the tape under your armpits. Breathe normally.
flow.parent: Read the tape at the front, where the two ends meet. Keep the tape level all the way round. A measurement is only good to about half a centimetre. No tape measure? Use a piece of string: pinch the string where the ends meet, lay it flat along a ruler or a metre scale and read the length. A soft tape from a stationery or tailoring shop costs about Rs 20 to 40. The string method is a little less exact, so repeat each reading once.
flow.context: In this step you set up the tape and practise reading it while the child breathes normally.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit straight and breathe quietly. At the end of a quiet breath out, read the tape. At the end of a quiet breath in, read it again. Repeat once more.
flow.say: Sit straight and breathe quietly. I will say now at the end of a breath out, and then at the end of a breath in.
flow.kid: Sit straight. Breathe quietly. A grown-up reads the tape at the end of each breath.
flow.parent: The quiet change is small, perhaps 1 centimetre. Look at the tape right at the end of the breath. If two readings differ by more than 1 centimetre, do a third.
flow.context: In this step you measure a quiet breath out and a quiet breath in.

flow.do: Ask the child to breathe out as far as is comfortable, and read the tape. Then ask for the deepest breath in, and read it again. Repeat once.
flow.say: Breathe out gently as far as is comfortable. Now breathe in as deep as you can. Hold it for a second while I read.
flow.kid: Breathe out. Now breathe in as deep as you can. Hold it for a second.
flow.parent: Do only two deep breaths in this step. Stop if the child feels dizzy. A big breath in an upright child grows the chest by about 3 to 6 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step you measure your deepest breath while sitting straight.

flow.do: Ask the child to slump forward over the knees, like looking at a phone. Repeat the breath out and the deepest breath in. Read the tape both times. Repeat once.
flow.say: Slump forward like you are looking at a phone. Breathe out, and then in as deep as you can.
flow.kid: Slump forward. Breathe out. Now breathe in as deep as you can.
flow.parent: Slumping usually makes the deepest breath smaller, because the ribs and diaphragm have less room. A child with a very deep slump may not see a difference. Report what you see.
flow.context: In this step you repeat the deepest breath while slumped, to see whether posture matters.

flow.do: Help the child work out the growth for each kind of breath. Ask for a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. Compare it with the first guess. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Subtract the small number from the big number for each breath. Which breath grew your chest the most? What does the tape show?
flow.kid: Subtract to find the growth. Which breath grew your chest the most?

check.q: After a quiet breath out the tape reads 62 cm. After a deepest breath in it reads 67 cm. How much did the chest grow?
check.why: To find how much the chest grew, take the smaller number away from the bigger one. 67 take away 62 is 5. If you chose 129, you added them.

ask.q: Why do you think the tape got longer when you breathed in?
good: Air went in and filled my lungs.

flow.parent: Many children are surprised by how little the chest moves in a quiet breath. Ask where the rest of the room for air comes from. The diaphragm moves down, and the belly moves out. The tape cannot see that.
flow.context: In this step you work out the growth for each kind of breath and decide what your numbers show.

activities.title: Two Clocks: which one can you steer?

materials.item: a phone or clock with a seconds hand

activities.safety: Hold your breath only for a few seconds, and only after a normal breath in. Never breathe fast and deep first.
activities.record: Write how many beats you counted in 15 seconds in each try. Write what you felt when you held your breath.
activities.context: In this activity, you listen to your heart and your breath for a minute. You try to change each one on purpose, and see which one obeys.

setup.art: A child sitting still with one hand on her wrist and one hand on her belly.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still. Put one hand on your wrist and one on your belly.

setup.art: The child trying to slow her heart by deciding, with a thought bubble that says slow down.
setup.caption: 2. Try to slow your pulse just by deciding.

setup.art: The child holding her breath with puffed cheeks and a grown-up counting seconds.
setup.caption: 3. Hold your breath for five seconds. Notice what your body does next.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit still for one minute. One hand rests on the wrist and one on the belly. Count the pulse for 15 seconds, and the breaths for 15 seconds.
flow.say: Sit still. One hand finds your pulse, and one hand rests on your belly. Count both for fifteen seconds.
flow.kid: Find your pulse. Feel your belly rise. Count both for 15 seconds.
flow.context: In this step you find your two clocks, the heartbeat and the breath, and count them.
flow.parent: One child: the parent times. With 2 to 4 children: everyone does the tries at the same time, each with their own pulse and breath, and one child is the timer. Compare the numbers afterwards.

flow.do: Ask the child to try to slow the heart by deciding, for 15 seconds. Count the pulse again. Then try to make the heart go faster by deciding, and count again.
flow.say: Now try to make your heart slow down, just by deciding. Count your pulse. Now try to make it speed up, just by deciding.
flow.kid: Try to slow your heart by deciding. Count. Try to speed it up. Count.

ask.q: Could you change your heartbeat just by deciding?
good: A little, if I thought of something scary.

flow.parent: Most children cannot change the count by more than 1 or 2 beats. If the child imagines something scary or exciting, the pulse may rise by a few beats. That is a different route from commanding the heart.
flow.context: In this step you try to steer your heart by deciding, and see what happens.

flow.do: Ask the child to breathe in normally and hold the breath for five seconds, while a grown-up counts. Then breathe out. Ask what the body wants to do next.
flow.say: Breathe in normally. Now hold it while I count to five. Breathe out. What did your body want to do?
flow.kid: Breathe in. Hold it while a grown-up counts to five. Breathe out.

ask.q: What did your body do when you held your breath?
good: I felt an urge in my chest.

ask.q: Which clock could you steer, the heart or the breath?
good: Only the breath, the heart did its own thing.

flow.parent: Hold for no more than 5 to 10 seconds. Never ask a child to breathe fast and deep first, because this can make a person faint. The urge to breathe is the body's own signal.
flow.context: In this step you hold your breath for a few seconds, and notice that your body wants to breathe again.

activities.title: Waiting for the Bell: does your pulse rise before you move?

materials.item: a phone or clock with a stopwatch
a chair
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: The child only waits and does not run in this activity. Keep a grown-up beside the child.
activities.record: Write the beats in 15 seconds for each calm count and each waiting count. Write whether the waiting count was higher each time.
activities.context: In this activity, you count your pulse while you sit calmly, and again while you wait for something exciting. You find out whether your heart starts before you do.

setup.art: A child sitting calmly on a chair, counting her pulse while a parent talks about the weather.
setup.caption: 1. Count your pulse while you sit calmly.

setup.art: The child sitting on the chair with a stair step in front of her, and a parent saying get ready, then holding a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Count again while you wait for a race that never starts.

setup.art: A notebook with three pairs of numbers, each pair circled.
setup.caption: 3. Repeat three times. Write all the pairs.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit calmly and chat about something ordinary for a minute. Then count the pulse for 15 seconds. Write the number as calm 1.
flow.say: Sit and tell me about your day. Then count your pulse for fifteen seconds. This is your calm count.
flow.kid: Sit and chat for a minute. Then count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse while you are calm. This is the number to compare with.
flow.parent: With more than one child, the child being tested should not see the trick. Send the others out of earshot, or let them be the counter or the timer and ask them to keep the secret. Then swap, so each child is tested once by a fresh trick.

flow.do: Tell the child that a race will start soon, up the stairs and down, and that you will say go. Wait 20 seconds in silence with the stopwatch visible. Count the pulse for 15 seconds, but never say go.
flow.say: In a moment, you will race up the stairs and back. Hands ready. Count your pulse now while we wait.
flow.kid: Get ready for a race. Count your pulse while you wait.

ask.q: What do you notice about your heart while you wait?

flow.parent: Do not start the race. Tell the child at the end that there is no race, and thank them for helping the test. This is a small trick, and it is fine to tell the child why.
flow.context: In this step you wait for a race that never starts, and count your pulse while you wait.

flow.do: Rest for two minutes. Repeat the pair of counts two more times. Put the calm count first in one pair and the waiting count first in another. Write all the pairs.
flow.say: We will do it again, twice more. Sometimes the calm count comes first, and sometimes the waiting count comes first.
flow.kid: Do it two more times. Write every pair of numbers.
flow.parent: Swapping the order makes the test fairer, because the pulse also changes with time. A rise of 1 to 3 beats in 15 seconds is typical. A difference of one beat could be a miscount, so look at whether the waiting count is higher in all three pairs.
flow.context: In this step you repeat the pairs twice more, in a mixed order, to see whether the result is steady.

flow.do: Look at the three pairs. Ask the child to say whether the waiting count was higher each time, and what that might mean. Do not explain before the child has answered.
flow.say: Look at your three pairs. Was your pulse higher while you waited? What do you think your body was doing?
flow.kid: Look at your three pairs. Was waiting higher each time? Why?

ask.q: Was the waiting count higher in every pair?
If it was higher, what might that mean?
good: My body got ready before I moved.

flow.parent: Be honest about the result. If the waiting count was higher in all three pairs, that is real evidence that the heart starts getting ready before the body moves. If it was mixed, the effect may be too small to count by hand, and that is also a true result.
flow.context: In this step you look at your pairs of numbers and decide what they show.

activities.title: The Pulse and the Breath: do they dance together?

materials.item: a phone or clock with a stopwatch
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Breathe slowly and gently and never strain. Stop if the child feels dizzy.
activities.record: Write the dots counted in the in-breaths and the out-breaths, and work out beats per 10 seconds for each. Write which was higher.
activities.context: In this activity, you breathe slowly and count your pulse during the in-breaths and the out-breaths. You look for a tiny speed-up and slow-down that scientists have found in young people.

setup.art: A child sitting still breathing in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6, while a parent counts aloud.
setup.caption: 1. Breathe in for a count of 4, and out for a count of 6.

setup.art: A parent holding the child's wrist and making a pencil dot on paper for every beat, with a short line drawn at each change from in to out.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up makes a dot for each heartbeat and a line when the breath changes.

setup.art: A paper strip of dots with lines, and the in-breath dots circled in one colour and the out-breath dots in another.
setup.caption: 3. Count the dots in the in-breaths and in the out-breaths.

flow.do: Ask the child to sit still and practise for one minute. Breathe in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6. A grown-up counts aloud.
flow.say: Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out slowly while I count to six. Let us practise for a minute.
flow.kid: Breathe in for a count of 4. Breathe out for a count of 6.
flow.parent: Counting aloud one number per second keeps the rhythm steady. Practise until the child can do it without strain.
flow.context: In this step you practise the slow breath, which makes the pulse and breath dance the most.

flow.do: A grown-up holds the child's wrist. For 50 seconds the child breathes in for 4 counts and out for 6 counts. The grown-up makes one pencil dot on paper for each beat. At each change of breath, the grown-up draws a short line.
flow.say: I will feel your pulse and make a dot for every beat. I will draw a line when you change from in to out. Keep your breathing slow and steady.
flow.kid: Breathe in for 4 and out for 6, five times. A grown-up dots your beats.
flow.parent: The child breathes five times, which takes about 50 seconds. The dots will fall into five in-sections and five out-sections. Do the whole round again if the dots get messy. Breathing with a spoken count keeps the rhythm steady. With two or three children: one breathes, one dots, and one counts aloud, then swap. A child can also dot their own beats with the free hand while a grown-up counts the breaths. If the pencil is too awkward, tap a finger on the table for each beat and let another person count the taps.
flow.context: In this step a grown-up marks your heartbeats on paper while you breathe slowly.

flow.do: Count all the dots in the five in-sections, and then all the dots in the five out-sections. Divide the in-breath dots by 2, since five in-breaths take 20 seconds. Divide the out-breath dots by 3, since five out-breaths take 30 seconds. Compare the two numbers.
flow.say: Five in-breaths took twenty seconds, so divide those dots by two. Five out-breaths took thirty seconds, so divide those dots by three. Which number is bigger?
flow.kid: Count the in-dots and the out-dots. Divide by 2 and by 3. Compare.

ask.q: Were there more beats for each 10 seconds while you breathed in or out?

flow.parent: Many families will see no difference, because the effect is a tiny speed-up and slow-down, and one missed dot can hide it. When it shows, the in-breath is a little faster. A heart monitor shows it clearly. Report what you see, and say whether it was the same on a second try. Do the whole round twice and add up the dots from both rounds before you divide, because more breaths make a tiny difference easier to see. If the two numbers are within one beat of each other, that is a normal result with hand counting, not a failure. A phone or watch with a pulse reader can show it more clearly.
flow.context: In this step you compare the in-breath and out-breath dots, and think about what they show.

activities.title: Clap the Animal Clocks: how fast is a heart?

materials.item: a phone or clock with a stopwatch
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Use only your hands to clap. Do not use sticks or bangers in the house.
activities.record: Write how many claps you made for each animal in 10 seconds, and how many the real heart would make. Write which one you could not do.
activities.context: In this activity, you clap the heartbeat of an elephant, a child and a cat. You find out how slow a big animal's heart is and how fast a small animal's heart is.

setup.art: A child clapping slowly, one clap every two seconds, next to a drawing of an elephant.
setup.caption: 1. Elephant: clap once every 2 seconds, for 10 seconds.

setup.art: The child clapping a little faster beside a drawing of a child, then fast beside a drawing of a cat.
setup.caption: 2. Child and cat: clap faster, for 10 seconds each.

setup.art: A drawing of a mouse and a hummingbird with the number of claps they would need in 10 seconds.
setup.caption: 3. Mouse and hummingbird: too fast to clap, so count the claps you would need.

flow.do: Clap the elephant. An elephant's heart beats about 30 times a minute, which is one beat every 2 seconds. Clap once every two seconds for 10 seconds. A grown-up counts the seconds.
flow.say: An elephant's heart beats about thirty times a minute. That is one beat every two seconds. Clap with me for ten seconds.
flow.kid: Clap once every 2 seconds, for 10 seconds. How many claps?

ask.q: How many claps did the elephant make in 10 seconds?

flow.context: In this step you clap the slow heart of an elephant.

flow.do: Clap the child's heart at about 85 beats a minute, which is 14 claps in 10 seconds. Then clap the cat's heart at about 150 beats a minute, which is 25 claps in 10 seconds. First count your own pulse for 10 seconds and compare it with 14, because 14 claps is only a typical number.
flow.say: Your heart beats about eighty-five times a minute, so about fourteen claps in ten seconds. A cat's heart beats about a hundred and fifty times a minute. Try twenty-five claps in ten seconds.
flow.kid: Clap 14 times in 10 seconds. Now clap 25 times in 10 seconds.

ask.q: Which was harder to clap, the child or the cat?
good: The cat was too fast to keep steady.

flow.parent: Twenty-five claps in ten seconds is hard to keep even. It is fine if the child gets close. With 2 to 4 children: one claps, one times, and one counts the claps aloud, then swap. Everyone can also clap together. Heart rates here are about figures for resting animals, and real animals vary.
flow.context: In this step you clap the heart of a child and a cat, and feel how much faster the cat's heart is.

flow.do: Work out how many claps a mouse and a hummingbird would need in 10 seconds. A mouse's heart beats about 600 times a minute, and a hummingbird's can reach about 1,200 times a minute in flight. Try to flutter your fingers as fast as you can for 10 seconds.
flow.say: A mouse's heart beats about six hundred times a minute. How many beats is that in ten seconds? A hummingbird's in flight can reach about twelve hundred times a minute. How many in ten seconds?
flow.kid: A mouse's heart beats 600 times a minute. How many beats is that in 10 seconds?

ask.q: How many beats would a mouse's heart make in 10 seconds?
Why do you think a small animal's heart beats faster than a big one's?
good: Small bodies burn food faster for their size.
Small hearts squeeze less blood at a time.

flow.parent: A mouse's heart makes 100 beats in 10 seconds, and a hummingbird's 200. Nobody can clap that fast, and that is the point. Reasons for the pattern are in the card on other bodies and other clocks.
flow.context: In this step you work out how fast a mouse's and a hummingbird's hearts beat, which are too fast to clap.

projects.title: A Day in Pulse: two days, two lines

materials.item: a phone or clock with a stopwatch
graph paper or squared paper
coloured pencils in two colours
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: The child only sits, stands and plays normally. Take the counts between normal activities and do not push the child to run.

schedule.what: Count your pulse at six moments in the day, and write each number.
Count at the same six moments again, draw both days as two lines, and compare.

projects.record: Write six pulse counts for each day, the time of each and what you were doing. Draw two lines on one graph.
projects.context: In this project, you count your pulse at the same six moments on two days. You draw both days as lines and see what changes during a day, and what stays the same.

setup.art: A child lying in bed at dawn, counting her pulse with a stopwatch on the pillow.
setup.caption: 1. Count your pulse first thing, lying in bed.

setup.art: The child counting her pulse right after playing in the courtyard.
setup.caption: 2. Count it after play, at lunch time and at bedtime.

setup.art: A graph with time of day along the bottom and beats per minute up the side, with two coloured lines.
setup.caption: 3. Draw one line for each day.

flow.do: Draw a table with six rows. The rows are waking in bed, after breakfast, at study time, right after play, after dinner, and in bed before sleep. Guess which will be highest and lowest.
flow.say: We will count your pulse at six moments today. Which moment do you think will be highest, and which lowest? Why?
flow.kid: Pick six moments in your day. Which will be highest? Which lowest? Why?

ask.q: At which moment do you think your pulse is highest, and why?

flow.context: This is the first step of the project. You make a table and guess before you count.
flow.parent: One child: the parent helps count at the moments the child is busy. With 2 to 4 children: each child keeps their own table and colour, and siblings count each other's pulse, which also gives a second counter. A school day or a holiday day can both work, but keep the two days alike so the lines can be compared.

flow.do: On the first morning, count the pulse for 15 seconds lying in bed before getting up. Write it in the first row. Then count again after standing for one minute.
flow.say: Before you get out of bed, find your pulse and count for fifteen seconds. Then stand up for a minute and count again.
flow.kid: Count your pulse in bed. Stand up for 1 minute. Count again.

ask.q: Was the pulse higher lying down or after standing up?

flow.parent: Standing usually raises the pulse by a few beats, because gravity pulls blood towards the legs. The lying-down number is often the lowest of the day.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse before you get out of bed, which is often the lowest number of the day.

flow.do: During the day, count the pulse at the other five moments. Count for 15 seconds, multiply by 4, and write it in the table. Write what you were doing.
flow.say: Through the day, stop at each of the moments in your table, count for fifteen seconds, and write the number.
flow.kid: Count your pulse at each moment. Write the number and what you were doing.
flow.parent: Count right after play, before the child sits down. Counts after meals are done sitting quietly for a minute first.
flow.context: In this step you count your pulse at four more moments during the day.

flow.do: On day 2, count at the same six moments. Then draw a graph with the time of day along the bottom and beats per minute up the side. Draw day 1 in one colour and day 2 in the other.
flow.say: Today we count at the same six moments. Then we draw both days on one graph, in two colours.
flow.kid: Count again at the same six moments. Draw both days on one graph.
flow.context: In this step you repeat the counts on the second day and draw both days as two lines.

flow.do: Look at the two lines together. Ask what is the same and what is different. Ask for a claim, the evidence and the reasoning about which moments were highest and lowest.
flow.say: Look at your two lines. What is the same on both days? What is different? What do you think caused each difference?
flow.kid: Look at your two lines. What is the same? What is different?

ask.q: What stayed the same on both days?
good: The highest point was after play.
The lowest point was in bed.

ask.q: What changed, and what do you think made it change?
good: I was more excited on one day.
I played harder on one day.

flow.parent: Expect the shape to be similar on both days, with the numbers differing by a few beats. Pulse wobbles by about 5 beats a minute from many small causes, so a small difference does not mean much.
flow.context: In this step you compare your two lines and decide what they show.

challenges.title: The Calm-Down Plan: bring a racing pulse down fastest
challenges.problem: After hard exercise, your pulse is racing. Design a routine of 45 seconds that brings it down as far as possible. Then count your pulse for 15 seconds, and test your routine against doing nothing but sitting.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
No medicines, no hot water and no ice.
Do not hold your breath, and never breathe fast and deep.
Test every plan after exactly the same exercise, with a full rest between tests.
The routine lasts 45 seconds. Then you count your pulse for 15 seconds.
general: Sit down and rest with the hands on the knees.
Lie down on a mat and close the eyes.
Walk slowly around the room instead of stopping.
creative: Breathe in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6, so the out-breath is longer.
Hum on every out-breath, which makes the out-breath longer without effort.
Hold a cool damp cloth against the face and neck while you sit.
Sit by a fan or open window while breathing slowly.
Do a short slow stretch and a slow breath together.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own 45-second routine. Test it against sitting still, using the same exercise and the same counts. Report which brought the pulse down further, and by how many beats.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the heart's brake. You try to bring a racing pulse down quickly, and test your ideas with real counts.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair counting her pulse after step-ups, with a stopwatch beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Do 45 seconds of step-ups. Sit and count your pulse.

setup.art: The same child doing slow breathing with a longer out-breath, with a parent counting out loud.
setup.caption: 2. After a full rest, repeat, but try your routine for 45 seconds.

setup.art: A notebook table with two rows, sit still and my routine, and the pulse after one minute.
setup.caption: 3. Count for 15 seconds, and compare the two tests.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Make a list of ideas for calming a racing pulse. Choose two ideas to test, plus sitting still as the comparison.
flow.say: After hard exercise, your pulse is racing. How could you bring it down quickly? Let us list ideas and pick two to test.
flow.kid: Your pulse is racing after exercise. How could you calm it? List ideas.

ask.q: What do you do when you want to calm down?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Calm-Down Plan challenge. You list ideas.

flow.do: Test sitting still. The child does 45 seconds of step-ups and sits straight down. After 45 seconds of sitting, count the pulse for 15 seconds. Write the number and multiply by 4.
flow.say: Do forty-five seconds of step-ups, then sit still for forty-five seconds. Then we count your pulse for fifteen seconds. This is the comparison.
flow.kid: Step for 45 seconds. Sit still for 45 seconds. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.parent: The count covers the 45 to 60 second window after stopping. Use the same window for every test. Stop at once if the child feels dizzy.
flow.context: In this step you test doing nothing but sitting, so you have a number to beat.

flow.do: After a full rest of at least 5 minutes, repeat the same step-ups. This time use the first idea for 45 seconds, then count the pulse for 15 seconds. Rest, and test the second idea in the same way.
flow.say: Same exercise, same count, but this time we try your idea. After a full rest, we try the second idea in the same way.
flow.kid: Rest. Step for 45 seconds. Try your idea. Count your pulse for 15 seconds.
flow.parent: The 5-minute rest is important, because an idea tested too soon will look better or worse than it really is. A fair test changes only the idea.
flow.context: In this step you test your ideas one at a time, with the same exercise and the same count.

flow.do: Compare the three numbers. Ask which idea brought the pulse down most. Ask the child to say how sure they are, given that counts wobble by a few beats.
flow.say: Which idea brought your pulse down the most? How many beats lower than sitting still? Are you sure, or could it be a wobble in the counting?
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? By how many beats? How sure are you?

ask.q: Which idea brought the pulse down the most, and by how many beats?
good: Sitting still was as good as anything.

ask.q: How could you make the test more trustworthy?
good: Ask another person to do the test.

flow.parent: A difference of fewer than 8 beats a minute could easily be counting error. An honest answer is that no idea beat sitting still by much, and that repeating the test would help. Later tests start a little tired, which can make them look worse. To check, sit still once more at the end and compare it with the first sit. With 2 to 4 children: each child tests their own plan, and one child times for all. Do not run the step-ups side by side. Keep the cloth cool and damp from the tap, never cold from the fridge.
flow.context: In this step you compare your results and decide how sure you can be.

items.p: Rani counts 18 beats in 10 seconds. How many beats per minute is that?
items.why: There are six 10-second spells in a minute. 18 times 6 is 108. If you chose 28, you added 10. If you chose 180, you multiplied by 10.

items.p: You should feel your pulse with your thumb, because the thumb has the strongest pulse.
items.why: False. The thumb has a pulse of its own, so you may count your own thumb's beat and not your wrist's. Use two fingers.

items.p: To turn a 15-second pulse count into beats per minute, you multiply by ____.
a: four
items.why: Four spells of 15 seconds make one minute, so the count is multiplied by 4.

items.p: What is the pulse that you feel at your wrist?
opts: A wave of stretch moving along the artery wall
The same blood from that beat arriving at the wrist
A muscle in the wrist twitching
items.why: The heart pushes blood into the arteries, and their elastic walls stretch. The stretch travels as a wave at 5 to 10 metres a second, much faster than the blood.

items.p: Put these steps in the right order for counting a fair pulse.
items: Count the taps for exactly 15 seconds
Find the pulse with two fingers
a: Sit quietly for two minutes
Find the pulse with two fingers
Count the taps for exactly 15 seconds
Multiply the count by 4
items.why: A fair count starts with a calm body. You then find the pulse, count for the same time every time, and finish with the sum.

items.p: Zainab's pulse was 80 beats per minute at rest and 112 beats per minute after 15 seconds of step-ups. By how many beats per minute did it rise?
items.why: 112 take away 80 is 32. So her pulse rose by 32 beats per minute in only 15 seconds.

items.p: In a pulse test, the first count after stopping is a little lower than the highest pulse during the exercise. Why?
opts: The pulse starts to fall the moment you stop
items.why: The brake on the heart comes back within seconds. By the time the first 15-second count is over, the pulse is already falling.

items.p: Match each part of the body to its job in breathing.
pairs: flattens downwards to make the chest bigger
lift the ribs up and out
hold the air and pass oxygen into the blood
carries air between the throat and the lungs
items.why: The diaphragm and the rib muscles do the work of making the chest bigger. The lungs have no muscles of their own, and they are filled by the air that flows in.

items.p: Sort each body job by who is in charge.
cats: Automatic, but I can take over
items: Automatic, but I can take over
Automatic, but I can take over
items.why: The heartbeat and digestion run by themselves and you cannot order them. Breathing and blinking run by themselves, and you can also do them on purpose. Choosing a word and pointing are decisions.

items.p: Here is a picture of a chest cut open at the side. Label the four parts.
a: Top, the tube going down the neck: windpipe
Large soft shape inside the chest: lung
Curved bone around the lung: rib
Dome-shaped muscle at the bottom: diaphragm
items.why: The windpipe brings air down into the lungs. The ribs form a cage round the lungs, and the diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle underneath.
items.art: A side view of a chest with a lung, ribs, windpipe and diaphragm, each with an empty label box.

items.p: Describe what happened to your pulse in the Pulse Timeline test. In which stretch did it change the most?
items.a: My pulse was 84 at rest. It rose to 108 after only 15 seconds of stepping, and to 140 after a minute. It changed the most in the first 15 seconds.
items.why: A strong answer uses real numbers from the test and names the stretch where the change was biggest. The first 15 seconds usually show the steepest rise.

items.p: Draw the shape of a pulse rising when exercise starts and falling when it stops. Mark with an arrow where it changes fastest.
items.a: A line that rises steeply at the start and then flattens, and then falls steeply after stopping and flattens again. The arrows point to the steepest parts.
items.why: A strong drawing shows steep parts at the beginning of the rise and at the beginning of the fall, with flatter parts after them.
items.art: An empty graph with time along the bottom and beats per minute up the side.

items.p: You held your breath for five seconds. What did your body want to do, and what does it tell you about who runs your breathing?
items.a: My body wanted to breathe. Breathing is run by my brainstem all the time, and I can take over for a short while, but the brainstem pushes me to breathe again.
items.why: A strong answer says that breathing is automatic, that you can steer it for a while, and that the body brings back the rhythm.

items.p: In a quiet breath, a tape round the chest grows only about 1 centimetre. Why does the tape not show all the extra room the lungs get?
opts: The diaphragm moving down adds room that the tape cannot see
The lungs do not grow when you breathe in
items.why: When the diaphragm moves down, it pushes the belly out and gives the lungs much of their new room. A tape round the chest only sees the ribs.

items.p: A transplanted heart, whose nerves have been cut, still beats.
items.why: True. The pacemaker cells start each beat themselves, so a heart with no nerves still beats. It beats faster at rest than a normal heart, because the nerve brake is missing.

items.p: What does the vagus nerve do to the heart?
opts: It sends signals that slow the pacemaker down
It makes the heart beat faster
It starts the first beat of the heart
items.why: The vagus nerve releases a chemical onto the pacemaker cells that makes them fire less often. The pacemaker itself starts the beats.

items.p: A person with a transplanted heart has a resting pulse of about 100. What does this suggest?
opts: Without the nerve brake, the heart beats at its own faster speed
New hearts are weak and need to beat faster
items.why: The transplant cuts the nerves. Without the brake, the pacemaker beats at its own speed, which is faster than most resting pulses.

items.p: The small patch of cells at the top of the heart that starts every beat is called the ____.
a: pacemaker
sinoatrial node
items.why: The pacemaker cells make a tiny electrical signal again and again. The signal spreads over the heart, which squeezes.

items.p: Your pulse rises in the first seconds of running mainly because your muscles have run out of oxygen.
items.why: False. The pulse rises within a second or two, long before the muscles run low. The first jump happens because the brake signals ease off.

items.p: Put these in order for what happens in the heart when a child starts to run.
items: Adrenaline and the gas nerves push the pulse higher
The pulse levels off at a higher steady rate
The pulse jumps up within a second or two
a: The brake signals ease off
The pulse jumps up within a second or two
Adrenaline and the gas nerves push the pulse higher
The pulse levels off at a higher steady rate
items.why: The brake is the quickest to change, which gives the first jump. The slower signals add more speed over the next minute.

items.p: Match each animal to about how fast the heart beats at rest.
items.why: The smaller the animal, the faster the heart usually beats. Small bodies lose heat quickly and burn food quickly.

items.p: A mouse's heart beats 600 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 10 seconds?
items.why: 10 seconds is one sixth of a minute. 600 divided by 6 is 100.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Pulling your hand off a hot tava, jumping at a loud bang, your leg kicking when the doctor taps your knee, or deciding to wave at a friend.
items.a: Deciding to wave. The other three are reflexes that happen without a decision.
items.why: A reflex is a very fast automatic reaction. Waving is a choice that starts in the thinking part of the brain.

items.p: Here is a made-up graph of a child's pulse. Between which two points does the pulse rise fastest for each second?
items.why: In the first 15 seconds the pulse rose by 24 beats, which is about 1.6 beats every second. Later it rose more slowly.

chart.title: A child's pulse during step-ups (made-up numbers)

items.p: Why is it dangerous to breathe fast and deep many times before holding your breath underwater?
opts: It lowers carbon dioxide, so the urge to breathe comes late and you can faint
It fills your lungs with too much air
items.why: The urge to breathe comes mostly from rising carbon dioxide. Fast deep breathing removes carbon dioxide, so the warning comes late, while oxygen can run low enough to make you faint.

items.p: The signal that a nerve sends to slow a heart is a chemical released at the heart.
items.why: True. In 1921, Otto Loewi showed that fluid from a slowed frog heart slowed a second heart that had no nerve. The chemical was later named acetylcholine.

items.p: In your own words, explain why a resting heart beats more slowly than its own pacemaker would. Use the word brake.
items.a: The pacemaker would beat at about 100 or more. A nerve called the vagus nerve sends steady signals that act like a brake and slow the pacemaker. At rest the brake is on, so the pulse is lower.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pacemaker has its own faster speed, that a nerve slows it, and that the brake is on at rest.

items.p: A hummingbird is tiny and a blue whale is huge. Give one reason their hearts beat at such different speeds.
items.a: A tiny hummingbird loses heat quickly and burns food very fast, so their cells need oxygen very fast and their heart beats over 1,000 times a minute. A blue whale is huge and can slow the heart to a few beats a minute when it dives.
items.why: A strong answer says that small bodies burn food faster for their size, so they need a faster heart. It may also say that a diving whale slows the heart to save oxygen.

items.p: Draw a side view of a chest breathing in and breathing out. Show the diaphragm and the ribs in both pictures.
items.a: Two pictures. Breathing in: the diaphragm is flat and the ribs are lifted. Breathing out: the diaphragm is domed upwards and the ribs are lower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the diaphragm flat and the ribs lifted for breathing in, and domed and lowered for breathing out.
items.art: Two empty side views of a chest, one labelled in and one labelled out.

items.p: Here is a picture of a heart with two nerves coming to it. Label what each part does.
a: Small patch at the top that starts each beat: pacemaker
Nerve that slows the pacemaker, the brake: vagus nerve
Nerve that speeds the pacemaker up, the gas: nerve that adds speed
items.why: The pacemaker starts the beats. The vagus nerve acts as a brake, and a second set of nerves, helped by adrenaline, acts as the gas.
items.art: A heart with a glowing patch at the top and two nerves reaching it, each with an empty label box.

items.p: Your pulse speeds up a little when you breathe in and slows down a little when you breathe out. Three friends argue about why.

views.who: Latha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: It helps the body. When the lungs are full of fresh air, more beats carry more oxygen round.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: It is an accident. The nerves that run breathing sit next to the nerves that run the brake, and some of the signal leaks across.

views.who: Dr Kavya, a heart doctor (an imagined view)
views.says: It may be a sign that the brake and the gas are working well. A heart that can change quickly is a flexible heart.

items.ask: Which idea would you most like to test? What could you measure to test it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one view, gives a reason, and suggests a test. For example, to test the first idea, measure how well the lungs swap gases when the heart follows the breath and when it does not.
items.why: Scientists still do not agree about the reason. A good answer shows that you can say what evidence would change your mind.

items.p: Priya counts 21, 22 and 29 beats in three counts of 15 seconds at rest. She wants one number for her resting pulse. What should she do, and why?
items.a: She should count again, because 29 is far from the other two and may be a miscount, or she may have moved. Then she can use the numbers that agree, such as 21 and 22, and say her pulse is about 86 beats per minute.
items.why: A strong answer spots the odd number, offers a reason, and uses repeated counts to get a trustworthy number. A miscount of one beat in 15 seconds is 4 beats per minute.

items.p: A child's heart beats 85 times a minute. About how many beats is that in one hour?
items.why: There are 60 minutes in an hour. 85 times 60 is 5,100.

items.p: After exercise, Kabir's pulse falls from 150 to 120 in the first minute. In the next minute it falls from 120 to 108. Explain why the second fall is smaller.
items.a: The brake on the heart comes back quickly, so the pulse falls fast in the first minute. After that the body is still warm and still has some adrenaline, so the pulse comes down slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says that the fast part of the fall is the brake returning, and that the slow part is the body winding down. The first fall was 30 beats and the second was 12.

items.p: Doctors give a rested grown-up a drug that blocks the vagus nerve. What do they find?
opts: The pulse rises towards the pacemaker's own speed of about 100
The pulse falls to nearly zero
items.why: If the brake is blocked, the pacemaker beats at its own speed. This is evidence that the vagus brake is on at rest.

items.p: The vagus nerve slows the heart by sending electricity straight into the heart muscle.
items.why: False. The nerve releases a chemical, acetylcholine, onto the pacemaker cells, and the chemical slows them.

items.p: A coach says: breathe slowly and calm your heart before the race. A rower says: I want my heart racing before the race, because it means I am ready.

views.says: Calm breathing helps you save energy for the long race and row to the drum.
My pulse rises before I move because my body is getting ready. That is good, so why fight it?
A rising pulse before a race is normal and useful. But if it makes you start too fast, a slower breath may help you keep to your plan.

items.ask: Whose view fits what you know about the pulse before exercise? What would you test to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer uses what is known, that the pulse rises before exercise because the brake eases, and suggests a test such as comparing race times with and without a slow-breathing routine.
items.why: All three views have something right. A strong answer says what each one gets right, and picks a test.

items.p: Sort each animal by whether the animal's resting heart beats faster or slower than a child's, which is about 85 beats a minute.
items.why: Small animals have fast hearts and large animals have slow hearts. A diving blue whale slows the heart to only a few beats a minute.

items.p: Why do insects not need blood to carry oxygen to their cells?
opts: Tiny air tubes carry air to every part of the body
Insects get oxygen from the food they eat
items.why: An insect breathes through small holes in the sides that lead to a branching system of air tubes, so the air reaches the cells directly.

items.p: Put these in the order they happen as you hold your breath.
items: Carbon dioxide slowly builds up in the blood
The brainstem forces you to breathe
a: You breathe in and hold
Carbon dioxide slowly builds up in the blood
Sensors notice the carbon dioxide
An urge to breathe grows
The brainstem forces you to breathe
items.why: Holding your breath lets carbon dioxide build up. Sensors notice it, and the urge grows until the brainstem takes over.

items.p: Many scientists once thought nerves could only make organs do more. What finding showed this was wrong, and why was it a surprise?
items.a: In 1845 two brothers, the Webers, sent a small current into the vagus nerve of a frog, and the heart slowed down. It was a surprise because people thought a nerve could only push an organ to work harder.
items.why: A strong answer says that a nerve was shown to slow an organ, and that this was a surprise because nerves were thought to make organs do more.

items.p: After a minute of step-ups, a child's pulse is 140. After one minute of rest it is 110. Before the step-ups it was 84. How many of the extra beats gained were lost in the first minute of rest?
items.why: The pulse rose from 84 to 140, which is 56 extra beats. After one minute of rest it was 110, so it had fallen by 140 take away 110, which is 30 beats.

items.p: Draw a diagram of the two routes that control your breathing. Use arrows to show the automatic route from the brainstem and the take-over route from the thinking part of the brain.
items.a: A brain with two arrows. One arrow goes from the brainstem to the breathing muscles, marked automatic. A second arrow goes from the top of the brain to the same muscles, marked I decide.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that both routes lead to the same muscles. This is why you can hold your breath, and why the body takes over again when you let go.
items.art: An empty outline of a head and chest with the breathing muscles marked in the chest.

items.p: Explain why you cannot hold your breath until you faint, and why it is still unsafe to breathe fast and deep first.
items.a: As carbon dioxide builds up, the urge to breathe becomes too strong and you breathe before you faint. But fast deep breaths wash carbon dioxide out of the blood, so the urge comes late, and the oxygen can run too low first.
items.why: A strong answer says that the urge comes from carbon dioxide, that it usually wins, and that overbreathing delays the warning.

items.p: Two children do the same step-ups. One has a pulse of 130 and the other has a pulse of 150. What is the best conclusion?
opts: Nothing yet, because people differ and counts wobble by a few beats
items.why: Heart rate after exercise varies from person to person for many reasons, such as age, size, how well they slept and how hard they stepped. One count cannot say who is healthier.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether your pulse rises while you wait for a race to start. Say what you would count, how often, and what you would keep the same.
items.a: I would count my pulse for 15 seconds while sitting calmly, and again while waiting for a race that never starts. I would do three pairs, change the order, and use the same wrist and the same time of day.
items.why: A strong answer compares a calm count with a waiting count, repeats the pair, mixes the order, and keeps the counting method the same.

quiz.p: You count 19 beats in 15 seconds. What is the pulse per minute?
quiz.why: There are four 15-second spells in a minute. 19 times 4 is 76. If you chose 34, you added 15.

quiz.p: Why does a resting heart beat more slowly than a heart with no nerves attached?
opts: A nerve keeps sending signals that slow the pacemaker
The heart is lazy when you rest
quiz.why: The vagus nerve acts like a brake on the pacemaker. A heart with no nerves attached beats at its own faster speed.

quiz.p: A child's pulse is 84 at rest, 108 after 15 seconds of step-ups and 140 after 60 seconds. When did the pulse rise the most for each second?
opts: It rose by the same amount each second
quiz.why: It rose by 24 beats in the first 15 seconds, which is about 1.6 beats a second. After that it rose by less than 1 beat a second (about 0.7), and then less.

quiz.p: What does your diaphragm do when you breathe in?
opts: It stays still while the lungs pull in air
quiz.why: The diaphragm flattens and the ribs lift, so the chest grows. The pressure inside falls and air flows in. The lungs have no muscle of their own.

quiz.p: If you are brave enough, you can hold your breath until you faint.
quiz.why: False. As carbon dioxide builds up, the urge to breathe becomes too strong, and you breathe before you faint. Never try to push through it.

quiz.p: Which of these is automatic, but you can also take over?
quiz.why: Breathing runs by itself in your sleep, and you can hold it, sigh or sing. You cannot order your heartbeat or your digestion.

quiz.p: A runner starts to run. What is the first change in the nerve signals to her heart?
opts: The heart stops for a moment
The lungs tell the heart to wait
quiz.why: The brake easing off gives the quick first jump in pulse within a second or two. Slower signals then add more speed.

quiz.p: The dome-shaped muscle under the lungs that flattens when you breathe in is the ____.
a: diaphragm
quiz.why: The diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing in. When it flattens, the chest gets bigger.

quiz.p: Which of these animals has the fastest heart at rest?
quiz.why: A mouse's heart beats about 600 times a minute. A child's beats about 85, and an elephant's about 30. Small bodies burn food faster for their size.

quiz.p: A frog's heart slows when the vagus nerve is stimulated. Which old idea did this surprise?
opts: That nerves can only make organs do more
quiz.why: Many scientists thought a nerve could only push an organ to work harder. The result showed that a nerve can also slow an organ.

quiz.p: A child counts 20, 21 and 29 beats in three counts of 15 seconds at rest. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Count again, because 29 is far from the other two
Use 29, because it is the biggest
quiz.why: A repeated count helps to find a number you can trust. A single count far from the others may be a miscount, or the child may have moved.

quiz.p: Three of these happen by themselves and one is a choice. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Pupils getting wider in the dark
quiz.why: Pupils, shivering and goosebumps are automatic. Waving is a decision that begins in the thinking part of the brain.

maths.problem: Three counts at rest were 20, 21 and 20 beats in 15 seconds. Then Dev counts 29 on the next try. Which is more likely to be right for his resting pulse, 84 or 116 beats per minute, and why?
maths.answer: 84 beats per minute is more likely.
maths.explain: 20, 21 and 20 times 4 give 80, 84 and 80. The count of 29 gives 116, which is far from the others. It was probably a miscount or came after he had moved. A mistake of one beat in 15 seconds is 4 beats a minute, so repeated counts are better than one.
maths.context: In the Pulse Timeline test, you count your pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by 4 makes a small counting mistake four times bigger, so repeating counts and comparing helps you trust a number.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of a child's pulse. How many beats a minute did it rise in the first 15 seconds, and how many in the next 45 seconds? Which stretch was faster?
maths.answer: 24 beats a minute in the first 15 seconds, and 32 beats a minute in the next 45 seconds. The first stretch was more than twice as fast.
maths.explain: From rest at 84 to 108 is 24. From 108 to 140 is 32. In the first stretch, 24 divided by 15 seconds is 1.6 beats each second. In the second, 32 divided by 45 seconds is about 0.7 beats each second. So the first stretch was more than twice as fast.
maths.context: In the Pulse Timeline test, you draw a line graph of your pulse after 15, 30 and 60 seconds of step-ups.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows how fast something changes. Comparing the rise per second in two stretches tells you where the change was quickest.

maths.problem: After a minute of step-ups, a child counts 44, 38, 34 and 31 beats in four 15-second windows in a row. What is the pulse in beats per minute for each window? How many beats a minute did it fall from the first window to the second, and from the third to the fourth?
maths.answer: 176, 152, 136 and 124 beats per minute. It fell by 24 from the first to the second, and by 12 from the third to the fourth.
maths.explain: 44 times 4 is 176, 38 times 4 is 152, 34 times 4 is 136, and 31 times 4 is 124. The fall from the first to the second is 176 take away 152, which is 24. The fall from the third to the fourth is 136 take away 124, which is 12. The fall slows down as the pulse comes back.
maths.context: In the Pulse Timeline test, you count four windows of 15 seconds straight after a minute of step-ups.
maths.why_maths: Turning each window into beats per minute puts them on the same scale, so you can compare how fast the pulse fell in each stretch.

maths.problem: A child's resting heart beats about 85 times a minute. About how many times does it beat in one whole day?
maths.explain: A day has 24 hours and each hour has 60 minutes, so a day has 24 times 60, which is 1,440 minutes. 85 times 1,440 is 122,400. So a child's heart beats more than a hundred thousand times every day.
maths.context: In the Pulse Timeline test, you work out your pulse in beats per minute.
maths.why_maths: A pulse in beats per minute is a rate. Multiplying by the minutes in a day shows how much work a heart does without ever being asked.

maths.problem: At rest, a child's heart pushes out about 40 millilitres of blood with each beat, and beats 85 times a minute. In hard exercise it pushes out about 55 millilitres and beats 160 times a minute. How much blood does it pump in a minute each way? How many times more is the exercise amount?
maths.answer: 3,400 millilitres at rest and 8,800 millilitres in exercise. That is about 2.6 times more.
maths.explain: At rest, 40 times 85 is 3,400. In exercise, 55 times 160 is 8,800. 8,800 divided by 3,400 is about 2.6. The heart does more by beating faster and by pushing out more blood with each beat.
maths.context: In the Pulse Timeline test, your pulse rises when you exercise.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two amounts as a ratio tells you how many times bigger one is than the other, which shows the combined effect of a faster pulse and a bigger push.

maths.problem: In the Chest Tape test, a child's chest measures 61 and 62 centimetres in a quiet breath. In a deepest breath it goes from 61 to 66 centimetres. Slumped, her deepest breath goes from 60 to 63 centimetres. How much did the chest grow in each, and how many times bigger was the deepest growth than the quiet growth?
maths.answer: 1 centimetre for quiet, 5 for deepest, and 3 for slumped. The deepest growth was 5 times the quiet growth.
maths.explain: 62 take away 61 is 1. 66 take away 61 is 5. 63 take away 60 is 3. 5 divided by 1 is 5. Sitting up straight gave 2 centimetres more growth than slumping, since 5 take away 3 is 2.
maths.context: In the Chest Tape test, you measure your chest after breathing out and after breathing in.
maths.why_maths: Taking one measurement away from another shows the change, and comparing the changes tells you which breath moved the chest most.

maths.problem: An elephant's heart beats about 30 times a minute, and a mouse's beats about 600 times a minute. In the 2 seconds between two elephant heartbeats, how many times does a mouse's heart beat?
maths.explain: The elephant's heart beats once every 2 seconds, since 60 divided by 30 is 2. In 2 seconds, a mouse's heart beats 600 divided by 30 times, which is 20. So a mouse's heart beats 20 times for each beat of an elephant's.
maths.context: In the activity Clap the Animal Clocks, you compare heart rates of different animals.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one rate by another tells you how many times faster one animal's heart is, which is a way to compare clocks that run at different speeds.

maths.problem: In the Pulse Timeline test, a child steps up once every 2 seconds for a full minute, and her pulse is 140 beats per minute at the end. How many step-ups did she make in the minute, and about how many heartbeats came for each step-up?
maths.answer: 30 step-ups, and between 4 and 5 heartbeats for each step-up.
maths.explain: One step every 2 seconds gives 60 divided by 2, which is 30 steps. 140 divided by 30 is a little under 5, about 4.7. So there were between 4 and 5 heartbeats for each step.
maths.context: In the Pulse Timeline test, you step up once every 2 seconds while your pulse climbs.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the heartbeats by the steps shows how hard the heart works for each movement of the body.

maths.problem: A made-up child counted her pulse at six moments in a day. Lying in bed it was 72. After breakfast it was 88. At study time it was 84. Right after play it was 132. After dinner it was 90. In bed before sleep it was 76. What is the difference between her highest and lowest, and which two moments were within 4 beats of each other?
maths.answer: The difference is 60 beats a minute. Lying in bed (72) and in bed before sleep (76) were 4 apart. Breakfast (88) and dinner (90) were 2 apart, and study time (84) and breakfast (88) were 4 apart.
maths.explain: The highest is 132 and the lowest is 72, and 132 take away 72 is 60. 76 take away 72 is 4. 90 take away 88 is 2, and 88 take away 84 is 4 as well. The sitting moments are all near each other, and play is far above them.
maths.context: In the project A Day in Pulse, you count your pulse at six moments in a day.
maths.why_maths: Finding the spread between the highest and lowest values, and which values sit close together, shows what changes a pulse and what does not.

applications: Doctors and nurses count the pulse and the breathing rate of every patient who comes to a clinic, because both numbers change quickly when someone is ill.
An electronic pacemaker, a small battery device, is placed in the chest of a person whose own pacemaker cells do not work well, and it starts every heartbeat for them.
A heart-rate monitor on a wrist or a finger clip shines a light through the skin and counts the pulse by the small changes in the light.
An ECG machine records the tiny electrical signals of the heart, and doctors read it to see whether the beat is steady.
Sports coaches ask athletes to count their resting pulse and how quickly it falls after hard exercise, to see how training is going.
Slow breathing exercises, such as long breaths out, are taught in yoga, in singing lessons and in some hospitals to help people calm down.
A defibrillator, found in some malls, airports and railway stations, gives an electric shock to restart a normal heartbeat.
Ventilators take over the job of the breathing muscles for people who cannot breathe well by themselves.
Free divers and swimmers train to use the dive reflex to slow the heart and save oxygen.
Anaesthetists watch the heart and breathing of every patient during an operation, because both can change when the brain's control is quietened.

open_questions.q: Why does the pulse speed up a little on every in-breath, and does that help the body?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have three main ideas, and none has been proved. It is hard to test, because the dance is hard to switch off.

open_questions.q: How does the thinking part of the brain take over a rhythm that the brainstem makes?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know which parts of the brain are involved, but not how a decision becomes a signal to a muscle.

open_questions.q: Is there a limit to how many heartbeats a body can have in a life?
open_questions.why_open: Many mammals have a similar number of heartbeats in a lifetime, but humans live much longer, and birds and bats break the pattern. Nobody agrees on the reason.

open_questions.q: How much does slow breathing change health over the long term?
open_questions.why_open: Slow breathing clearly changes pulse and calm in the short term. Longer studies are still small, and results are mixed.

open_questions.q: How do heart cells that touch fall into the same rhythm?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that cells pass tiny electrical signals through small openings between them, but they are still working out how thousands of cells agree on a rhythm.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the body know to ease the brake just before a race starts?
open_questions.why_open: The rise before exercise is well known, but the paths in the brain that start it are still being mapped.
