how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought a nerve could only make an organ do more. A nerve to a muscle makes it squeeze, so a nerve to the heart ought to make it beat faster. In 1845, two brothers in Germany, Ernst Heinrich Weber and Eduard Weber, tested this on frogs. They sent a small electric current into the vagus nerve, a nerve that runs to the heart. The heart did not speed up. It slowed down, and sometimes it stopped. Nobody knew how a nerve could do this. In 1921, Otto Loewi in Graz, in Austria, took two frog hearts. When he stimulated the vagus nerve of the first heart, it slowed. He then poured the salty water that had bathed the first heart onto the second heart, which had no nerve. The second heart slowed too. So the nerve had released a chemical. Loewi later said the idea came to him in a dream. The chemical was named acetylcholine.
how_we_found_out.who: Ernst Heinrich Weber and Eduard Weber, and Otto Loewi, with later work by Henry Dale
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought a nerve could only make an organ do more, and that a nerve spoke to an organ only with electricity. The Weber brothers showed a nerve could slow a heart, and Loewi showed that the slowing signal was a chemical.

roots.context: We have counted pulses and measured breaths. Now we ask what a heart that keeps its own time, and a breath that we can borrow, tell us about who we are and what a body is.

deep_truth.truth: Left alone, a heart beats more than 100 times a minute. A steady signal along a nerve from your brain slows it. Speeding up starts with that signal easing, before anything is added.
deep_truth.habit: We think of rest as the plain, natural state, and effort as something added on top. For the heart, it is the other way round. A resting heart is a heart being held back, and speeding up begins by taking something away.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Pulse Timeline test, most of the rise in pulse came in the first 15 seconds, long before the muscles ran short of oxygen. A transplanted heart, with its nerves cut, beats faster at rest than a normal heart. Frog hearts slowed by the vagus nerve gave Otto Loewi the same answer in 1921.

three.who_am_i: The signal that holds your heart back is made by your own body without you asking. 'You' includes a great deal that you never decide.
three.what_is_life: A living heart makes its own rhythm. Taken out of a frog and put in the right salty water, the heart goes on beating. Rhythm is part of what being alive is.
three.what_is_this_world: Heartbeats, breaths, days and tides are all rhythms. Living bodies keep their own time, and keep it in step with the world around them.

roots.thread: Your heart is made of billions of cells, and each one can beat alone. In the pacemaker, cells that touch fall into one shared rhythm, and the whole heart beats as one. A nerve from the brain then adjusts that single beat, and the lungs next door keep a rhythm that is linked to it. Many cells become one beat, and one beat is steered by something wider than the heart. That is how a body is a single thing made of many.

teachings.teaching: No mortal lives by the in-breath or the out-breath alone. They live by something else, on which both of these depend.
teachings.link: In this unit, the rhythm of breath comes from cells in the brainstem, and both the in-breath and the out-breath depend on them. The old verse also points to something behind the breath.

teachings.teaching: Some people offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, and so hold the course of both. This practice is called pranayama.
teachings.link: Breathing is the one automatic job we can steer, and many traditions noticed that long ago. The science of the longer breath out and the calmer pulse is a modern way of meeting the same practice.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, Peace Is Every Step, 1991
teachings.teaching: Breathing in, I calm my body. Breathing out, I smile.
teachings.link: A longer breath out is one of the few ways we can steer the heart's brake, and the tests in this unit are a way to see that it can work.

science.text: Heart cells grown alone in a dish each beat at their own pace. When they touch, they fall into one shared rhythm.
How the thinking part of the brain takes over an automatic rhythm, and what makes a choice feel like mine, is not known.

other_view.who: Most neuroscientists, and the old Indian Charvaka school
other_view.view: The pacemaker, the brake and the choice to hold a breath are all signals between cells. There is no extra 'you' beyond the body who steers. The feeling of being the one who chooses is itself something the brain makes. This is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.title: A longer breath out
practice.say: Sit comfortably and find your pulse with two fingers. Breathe in through your nose for four counts. Breathe out slowly for six counts. Do this five times. Notice whether your pulse feels any different. Then notice who is breathing, you or your body.
practice.kid: Sit still. Find your pulse. Breathe in for 4 counts. Breathe out for 6 counts. Do it five times. Does your pulse feel different? Who is breathing, you or your body?

ask: When you hold your breath, who is holding, and who is gasping? Are they both you?
If the brake on your heart is on even while you sleep, is that something you do, or something that is done to you?
Do heart cells that fall into the same beat when they touch know about each other? How would you find out?

playtest: Read as a parent and a child in a city flat would use it, but not yet done with a real child at home. Pulse Timeline: the step needs to be low and firm, and the 15-second step-up round, the 30-second round and the 60-second round each need about 2 to 3 minutes of rest, so the whole test takes close to an hour, and the spine counts it as the one long investigation. Counts wobble by one or two beats, so look at the shape of the curve and not single numbers. The rise should be easy to see (about 20 to 30 beats a minute in the first 15 seconds), and the recovery windows should fall steadily. If a child cannot count a fast pulse, a grown-up can count the neck pulse, or the child can count for 10 seconds and multiply by 6. Chest Tape: a quiet breath moves the tape by only about 1 centimetre, so read it right at the end of each breath and repeat once. Slumping usually, but not always, shrinks the deepest breath. Waiting for the Bell: the effect is small, perhaps 1 to 3 beats in 15 seconds, and it may not show in every family. That is a true result, and the activity says so. Pulse and Breath Dance: many families will not see a difference by hand. Who Is in Charge: all 24 cards were checked against the three kinds, and the game works for one player by answering aloud. Facts checked: the blue whale rates (2 beats a minute in dives, up to 37 at the surface, Goldbogen 2019) and the Weber brothers' 1845 frog result were confirmed online.
